lessonTitle: Prescribing in Clinical Scenarios: Fluids, Analgesia, Anticoagulants and Insulin

blocks.text: A man made nil by mouth for bowel surgery is left on a drip of 5% glucose for four days because nobody wrote a daily fluid plan. His sodium falls and he becomes confused. Nothing dramatic was prescribed, only something plain and then forgotten, which is exactly how many serious prescribing problems arise.

blocks.markdown: Fluids, analgesia, anticoagulants and insulin are among the most commonly prescribed and most frequently harmful medicines in hospital. Each combines a **narrow margin for error** with **patient-specific factors** (kidney function, weight, comorbidity) that must be checked every time. This unit teaches a safe, structured approach to each scenario. All doses and volumes are **teaching examples** based on widely used UK guidance (for example NICE guidance on intravenous fluids and the British National Formulary), not advice for any individual patient; always follow current local protocols and seek senior or pharmacist advice.

blocks.title: A safe prescribing routine
blocks.text: Before you prescribe: confirm the patient and allergy status; know the indication; check weight, kidney function and relevant results; look up the drug, dose, route and cautions; write clearly with units in full; state review or stop criteria; and arrange monitoring.

blocks.markdown:
### Intravenous fluids for a patient who is nil by mouth

A patient who cannot eat or drink needs **maintenance fluid** to replace daily losses, and may also need replacement of ongoing losses (for example vomiting or drains) or **resuscitation** if hypovolaemic. These are three distinct jobs: **resuscitation**, **replacement** and **maintenance**, and each should be prescribed deliberately. Assess volume status (history, observations, fluid balance charts, examination) and baseline blood tests (urea and electrolytes) before prescribing, and **reassess at least daily**.

NICE guidance for adults who need maintenance fluid suggests approximately **25 to 30 mL/kg/day of water**, and about **1 mmol/kg/day each of sodium, potassium and chloride**, and **50 to 100 g/day of glucose** to limit starvation ketosis. A balanced crystalloid is used for resuscitation, usually as a bolus of 500 mL given over less than 15 minutes, followed by reassessment. Caution is needed (for example lower volumes) in older, frail patients and in those with heart failure, kidney disease or malnutrition.

blocks.caption: The three fluid tasks
rows: Resuscitation
Restore circulating volume in shock or hypovolaemia
Crystalloid bolus 500 mL over less than 15 minutes, then reassess
Replacement
Replace ongoing losses and existing deficits
Match the fluid type to the loss, and prescribe the volume separately; record outputs
Maintenance
Meet daily water and electrolyte needs while nil by mouth
About 25-30 mL/kg/day water with sodium, potassium and glucose requirements; review daily

blocks.title: Prescribing maintenance fluid
blocks.prompt: A 70 kg man is nil by mouth after surgery, is haemodynamically stable, and has normal kidney function and electrolytes. Using 25 mL/kg/day of water and 1 mmol/kg/day of potassium (teaching example), calculate the daily volume, the hourly rate and the daily potassium requirement, and state what else you would specify.

steps.text: Daily water: 25 mL/kg/day x 70 kg = 1750 mL/day.
Hourly rate: 1750 mL / 24 hours = 72.9 mL/h, so about 73 mL/h (or prescribe in bags, for example 1 litre over a defined number of hours, per local practice).
Potassium: 1 mmol/kg/day x 70 kg = 70 mmol/day, usually provided as potassium in the maintenance bags and checked against the blood potassium result.

Specify the fluid type (for example a balanced crystalloid with glucose and electrolyte content that meets the requirements), the volume and rate, the start time and the review time, and note that urea and electrolytes and a fluid balance chart will be reviewed daily.
Reassess: if the patient becomes hypotensive, tachycardic or oliguric, this is resuscitation or replacement rather than maintenance, so reassess and escalate.

blocks.answer: About 1750 mL per day at roughly 73 mL/h with around 70 mmol potassium per day, prescribed as a specified fluid with a review time and daily blood tests.

blocks.title: Hospital-acquired hyponatraemia
blocks.text: Hypotonic fluids such as 5% glucose alone, given for several days, can cause dangerous hyponatraemia. Always specify the fluid, volume and rate, and recheck electrolytes.

blocks.markdown:
### Analgesia: matching the drug to the patient

Use a stepwise approach (the **WHO analgesic ladder** is a useful framework): start with **regular paracetamol** (adjusting the dose for low body weight and liver impairment), add a **non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)** only if there are no contraindications, and use **opioids** for moderate to severe pain with the lowest effective dose and monitoring. Always ask about allergies, comorbidity and kidney function, and prescribe a laxative with regular opioids.

blocks.caption: Choosing analgesia by comorbidity and kidney function
rows: Chronic kidney disease or acute kidney injury
NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion and may worsen kidney function; some opioids (for example morphine) have active metabolites that accumulate
Avoid NSAIDs; if an opioid is needed, use a reduced dose or longer interval and seek pharmacist advice on the choice
Heart failure or ischaemic heart disease
NSAIDs can cause fluid retention and increase cardiovascular risk
Avoid or use with great caution
Previous peptic ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, anticoagulation
NSAIDs increase gastrointestinal bleeding risk
Avoid NSAIDs; use paracetamol first
Asthma with NSAID sensitivity
NSAIDs can trigger bronchospasm
Avoid NSAIDs
Older, frail, or respiratory disease
Opioid sedation and respiratory depression
Start low, titrate carefully and monitor sedation and respiratory rate
Low body weight (below 50 kg) or hepatic impairment
Paracetamol toxicity risk
Reduce the paracetamol dose according to the BNF

blocks.title: Choosing analgesia
blocks.prompt: A 78-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (stage 4), heart failure and previous gastric ulceration has a fractured wrist awaiting surgery. She is in moderate pain. Select an approach.

steps.text: Check allergies and weight (to adjust paracetamol if below 50 kg) and recent kidney function results.
Start with regular paracetamol at the appropriate dose, as it is safe across kidney disease, heart failure and ulcer history.
Exclude NSAIDs: kidney disease, heart failure and previous gastric ulceration are three separate contraindications.

If paracetamol is insufficient, consider a low-dose opioid chosen with kidney function in mind and with pharmacist or senior advice, with reduced dose or extended interval, and monitor sedation and respiratory rate.
Add a laxative, review pain scores regularly and document the plan and review time.

blocks.answer: Regular paracetamol, no NSAID, and a carefully chosen low-dose opioid only if needed, with monitoring, a laxative and pharmacist advice.

blocks.markdown:
### Insulin and anticoagulants: high-risk medicines

Both insulin and anticoagulants are classified as **high-alert medicines**: errors can cause severe harm or death. The safety checks below are not optional extras.

blocks.caption: Safety checks for insulin and anticoagulant prescriptions
rows: Insulin

Name the exact insulin product (type and brand, as formulations differ); write 'units' in full; check capillary blood glucose and the indication; never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes without senior advice, because of the risk of ketoacidosis; use the correct insulin syringe or pen; follow local variable-rate infusion protocol
Writing 'U' or 'IU' (misread as zero or 10); prescribing 'insulin' without product; using a standard syringe; omitting insulin when the patient is nil by mouth
Heparins (for example low molecular weight heparin)
Indication and bleeding risk; weight and kidney function; platelet count and baseline clotting; timing relative to surgery or neuraxial procedures; dose by local protocol
Wrong weight-based dose; renal impairment not considered; dose not reviewed as kidney function changes
Warfarin
Indication, target INR range and planned duration; baseline and daily INR; interacting drugs; bleeding risk; give at a set time of day
No INR checked before the dose; wrong target; missing interaction (for example some antibiotics)
Direct oral anticoagulants
Indication; kidney function and weight; interacting drugs; correct drug-specific dose
Wrong dose for renal function; duplicate anticoagulants

blocks.title: Safety checking an anticoagulant prescription
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old woman admitted with leg cellulitis is to be given prophylactic low molecular weight heparin. Her weight is 52 kg, she has an estimated creatinine clearance that is reduced, and she takes an antiplatelet drug. Describe the safety checks you would make before prescribing.

steps.text: Confirm indication: venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, after a risk assessment of both clotting and bleeding risk.
Check bleeding risk factors: recent bleeding, low platelet count, active ulcer, upcoming procedures, and the interacting antiplatelet drug, which adds to the bleeding risk.

Check weight (52 kg) and kidney function, because low weight and reduced clearance affect dosing and accumulation; look up the product-specific advice in the BNF or local protocol, or ask the pharmacist.
Check baseline blood results: full blood count including platelets, and clotting if indicated.
Write the prescription with the drug name, dose, route, timing, indication and a review date, and arrange monitoring and follow-up of renal function and platelets.

blocks.answer: Check the indication, bleeding risk, weight, kidney function and baseline blood tests, look up dose adjustments, and prescribe with review and monitoring.

blocks.title: Write 'units', never 'U'
blocks.text: In OSCEs and in practice, the safest way to write insulin doses is '10 units' in full, with the named insulin and the time of administration. Check blood glucose before and after, and know what to do with insulin if the patient is nil by mouth.

points: For nil-by-mouth patients, separate resuscitation, replacement and maintenance, prescribe a specified fluid, volume and rate (about 25-30 mL/kg/day water in the teaching example), and review with blood tests at least daily.

Select analgesia using comorbidity and renal function: start with regular paracetamol, avoid NSAIDs in kidney disease, heart failure, ulcer history or anticoagulation, and use opioids cautiously with monitoring and a laxative.
Insulin and anticoagulants are high-alert drugs: name the product, write units in full, check glucose or INR, weight, renal function, bleeding risk and interactions, and specify monitoring.

questions.stem: How should a prescriber write a dose of ten units of insulin on a drug chart?

options.text: '10 units' written in full, with the named insulin product

questions.correctOptionText: '10 units' written in full, with the named insulin product

distractorRationale.a: Correct: unambiguous and identifies the product.
distractorRationale.b: 'U' can be misread as zero, giving 100 units.

questions.explanation: Writing 'units' in full avoids misreading abbreviations that have caused ten-fold overdoses. Naming the product matters because insulins differ in their duration and action.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with acute kidney injury and heart failure has moderate pain after a fall. Which analgesic is most appropriate to start?

options.text: Regular paracetamol at a dose appropriate to his weight
No analgesia because of the risks

questions.correctOptionText: Regular paracetamol at a dose appropriate to his weight

distractorRationale.a: Correct: safe first-line choice in kidney injury and heart failure.
distractorRationale.b: NSAIDs can worsen kidney injury and fluid retention.
distractorRationale.c: Morphine metabolites can accumulate in kidney injury, and unmonitored high doses are unsafe.
distractorRationale.d: Untreated pain is also harmful; safe options exist.

questions.explanation: NSAIDs are avoided in acute kidney injury and heart failure, and opioids need careful dosing in kidney impairment. Paracetamol, dosed to weight, is the safest first step.

questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation is admitted with a chest infection and is prescribed a new antibiotic. Which check is most important before the next warfarin dose?

options.text: Check the current INR and whether the new antibiotic interacts with warfarin
Check only the date of the last dose

questions.correctOptionText: Check the current INR and whether the new antibiotic interacts with warfarin

distractorRationale.a: Correct: INR guides dosing and interactions can raise INR and bleeding risk.
distractorRationale.b: Height does not affect warfarin dosing.
distractorRationale.c: The date of the last dose is not sufficient.
distractorRationale.d: Stopping without checking risks stroke and ignores the indication.

questions.explanation: Warfarin dosing depends on the INR, and many antibiotics alter its effect. Checking both prevents under- or over-anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 60 kg woman with type 1 diabetes is made nil by mouth before surgery. Which is the safest approach to her insulin?

options.text: Continue background insulin according to the local peri-operative protocol with glucose monitoring, seeking senior or diabetes team advice
Stop all insulin until she eats
Give her usual dose of mealtime insulin only
Do not check glucose because she is not eating

questions.correctOptionText: Continue background insulin according to the local peri-operative protocol with glucose monitoring, seeking senior or diabetes team advice

distractorRationale.a: Correct: people with type 1 diabetes need some insulin continuously to prevent ketoacidosis.
distractorRationale.b: Stopping all insulin risks diabetic ketoacidosis.
distractorRationale.c: Mealtime insulin without meals risks hypoglycaemia and omits background cover.
distractorRationale.d: Glucose should be monitored more closely, not less.

questions.explanation: People with type 1 diabetes lack endogenous insulin, so stopping background insulin can cause ketoacidosis within hours. Fasting patients need a plan that provides insulin, glucose and monitoring, usually with specialist input.

questions.stem: True or false: a patient who is nil by mouth should always receive 5% glucose alone as maintenance fluid for as many days as necessary.
questions.explanation: Prolonged hypotonic fluid can cause hyponatraemia, and maintenance fluids should supply water, sodium, potassium and glucose in suitable amounts. The plan must be reviewed daily with blood tests.

questions.stem: A 64 kg adult is nil by mouth and stable. Using 25 mL/kg/day as the maintenance water requirement (teaching example), calculate the total maintenance volume for 24 hours, in mL.
questions.explanation: Multiply the weight by the rate: 64 kg x 25 mL/kg/day = 1600 mL per day. This gives the starting volume, which must then be adjusted for losses, kidney function and frailty and reviewed daily.

questions.stem: The same 64 kg adult has been prescribed a maintenance volume of 1600 mL over 24 hours. Calculate the infusion rate in mL per hour (to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Divide the daily volume by the hours: 1600 mL / 24 h = 66.7 mL/h. In practice the nurse sets the pump or the bag duration to approximate this rate.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman is nil by mouth awaiting surgery, has stage 3 chronic kidney disease and has vomited several times. Explain how you would approach prescribing her intravenous fluids.
markingGuide: Assesses volume status with history, observations, examination, fluid balance and urea and electrolytes
Separates resuscitation, replacement of ongoing losses and maintenance
Resuscitation if hypovolaemic: bolus of crystalloid (for example 500 mL over less than 15 minutes) with reassessment
Maintenance calculated by weight (about 25-30 mL/kg/day water) with cautious, lower volumes in older and renally impaired patients, including sodium, potassium and glucose as appropriate
Specifies fluid type, volume, rate, start and review times
Monitors fluid balance and electrolytes at least daily and rethinks the plan if the patient changes
questions.explanation: Fluid prescribing is a clinical decision made on assessment, not a default bag. Older patients with kidney disease are at risk both of dehydration and fluid overload, so careful reassessment is essential.

questions.stem: Describe the safety checks you would make before prescribing insulin and before prescribing an anticoagulant, and explain why these are classed as high-risk medicines.
markingGuide: High-risk because errors can cause severe harm or death (hypoglycaemia or ketoacidosis; haemorrhage or thrombosis)
Insulin: exact product named, 'units' written in full, glucose checked, correct syringe or pen, background insulin not omitted in type 1 diabetes, follow local protocol
Anticoagulant: indication and bleeding risk, weight, kidney function, platelets and baseline clotting
Warfarin: target INR, current INR, interacting drugs, set time of day
Check for interactions and duplicate therapy
Specifies monitoring and review, with pharmacist or senior advice where needed
questions.explanation: Both drug groups have narrow margins between benefit and harm, so safety depends on specific checks that are done every time. Naming the checks and the reason for each demonstrates safe prescribing habits.

questions.stem: Explain how a patient's comorbidities and renal function influence the choice of analgesia, using at least three examples.
markingGuide: Chronic kidney disease or acute kidney injury: avoid NSAIDs; caution with opioids whose metabolites accumulate, so reduce dose or extend interval
Heart failure or ischaemic heart disease: NSAIDs cause fluid retention and cardiovascular risk
Peptic ulcer history or anticoagulant use: NSAIDs raise bleeding risk
Asthma with NSAID sensitivity: avoid NSAIDs
Older or respiratory disease: opioid sedation and respiratory depression, so start low and monitor
Low weight or liver impairment: reduced paracetamol dose
Paracetamol is a common safe first step; add laxatives with opioids
questions.explanation: The same drug can be safe in one patient and harmful in another, so choice depends on kidney function, comorbidity and other medicines. Linking each factor to the mechanism of harm makes the answer persuasive.
